title: NHL Analysis
text:
It is currently olympic hockey season, which means a hiatus from the regular NHL season as the best players fight it out for a Gold medal. This is a pivotal time for teams to be looking at other NHL teams performance and likely playoff brackets.
Lets first look at the league as a whole, to see who the big contenders are. Moneypuck.com is an extremely comprehensive NHL statistics project by Peter Tanner, with many useful already calculated statistics like expected goals for each situation.









These are the teams sorted by how many more goals they are expected to score than than their opponent. Colorado unsurprisingly has the highest expected goal differential, which isn’t at all surprising as they had a very dominant start to the season. I am a little surprised that teams like Florida are as high as they are as they have struggled this season despite their previous two years of postseason success. While coloring is not at all necessary here in this diverging lollipop plot, it does make it even clearer that a a high expected goal differential is better as it is green, helping those who may not have an extremely detailed hockey understanding to interperet this.
This is all useful to look at the league as a whole, but lets rank these by division as teams compete within their division in the playoffs.









Now we can see that even though the Vegas Golden Knights are 4th in the league for expeted goal differential, they are top of the pacific division, meaning that by this metric, they are are the most powerful team in their division, and would be the favorite to beat whoever they match up with in the first round. While color could be used to show divisions, it is much clearer when comparing within the division when the division is instead used to facet. Because of this, I have yet again used a diverging color scheme to help the reader understand that having a higher expected goal differential is better.

title: NFL Analysis
text:
How does change in ownership of an NFL impact the team?
If we take every team and look at how many wins they had each season, we can see how well each team did each season.
First, lets look at how many times teams have won









This isn’t a very helpful visualization on its own but I want to have this here as multiple later visuals are based on this.
Let’s take this data and look at it by team using a violin plot.









You see little some teams have clumps lower than each other but we need to see this information through time to be able to see if change in ownership was beneficial
To see this, lets take the first plot and highlight each team after they were sold. Lets also use team colors instead of a sequential or diverging theme. This is much more helpful than before. You can see the LA Rams have been on a steep upword trend after their acquisition, contrasting this, the Miami Dolphins haven’t been doing great since their sale in 2008. But how can we see if these teams have been improving since selling?









IS SELLING A TEAM GOOD FOR THEIR RECORD
Lets also add linear smoothers for before sale (green), and after sale (red), to see if teams are improving.









We can see clearly now that teams after selling have an upward trend whereas before selling, they tended to be stagnant.
Now, lets look at if each team improved since selling, or have some struggled?









Now we can see for each team that has sold in recent NFL history what teams have improved since selling. There is a clear trend that almost every team has a much steeper upward trajectory after sale. Why could this be? My speculation is owners sell the team when they lose interest. A new owner means renewed interest in the team financially and a general committment to better the team.

title: NHL Shot Analysis
text:
In this project, I used two primary data sources covering the 2025-26 NHL season. The first is a play by play dataset obtained through the R package nhlscraper which contains event level information about every game, including shot attempts, goals, penalties, and game context. The second data source is from Moneypuck.com and includes shot-locations through x y rink coordinates, event type, team identifiers, and period information for every recorded shot of the same season.
From the play by play data, I focus on events where a shot was taken or a goal was scores, and use variables such ad gameId, isHome, period, shotType, strengthState, and rink coordinates (xCoord, yCoord). Other features are created such as attacking side, estimated angle to the net, and the distance to the net. From the Moneypuck data, I use the adjusted coordinates, event type, home/away team codes, and an indicator for if the event resulted in a goal.
Both data sources index games differently. Moneypuck uses a game_id starting at 1 for each season, and the play by play data uses a gameId starting at 2025000001. Mapping these together allows the Shiny app and visualizations to filter consistantly by game and combine angle information with precise shot coordinates.


To look at these patterns across all games in the 2025-26 NHL season, I build a Shiny app that links the two data sources and lets the user pick any home and away team, select a specific game between them, and filter by period and shot result (GOAL, SHOT, MISS). For the selected settings, the app updates three views: An intercative shot map with shooting angles, a shot-density heatmap, and a bar chart of shot events by period and team.

shots_df <- read_csv(here("Data/shots_2025.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

period_labels <- c(
  "1" = "Period 1\nVAN 3 - COL 2",
  "2" = "Period 2\nVAN 6 - COL 3",
  "3" = "Period 3\nFinal: VAN 8 - COL 6"
)

avs_vs_canucks <- shots_df |>
  filter(
    homeTeamCode == "COL",
    awayTeamCode == "VAN",
    game_id == 21188,
    period %in% c(1, 2, 3),
    event %in% c("SHOT", "GOAL")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    team_label = case_when(
      teamCode == "COL" ~ "Colorado",
      teamCode == "VAN" ~ "Vancouver",
      TRUE ~ teamCode
    ),
    event_label = case_when(
      event == "GOAL" ~ "Goal",
      event == "SHOT" ~ "Shot",
      TRUE ~ event
    ),
    period_lab = factor(
      as.character(period),
      levels = c("1", "2", "3"),
      labels = period_labels
    )
  ) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(arenaAdjustedXCord),
    !is.na(arenaAdjustedYCord)
  )

goal_df <- avs_vs_canucks |>
  filter(event == "GOAL")





team_colors <- c(
  "Colorado" = "#6F263D",
  "Vancouver" = "#00843D"
)

geom_hockey(league = "NHL") +
  geom_point(
    data = avs_vs_canucks,
    aes(
      x = arenaAdjustedXCord,
      y = arenaAdjustedYCord,
      color = team_label
    ),
    alpha = 0.75,
    size = 2.8
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ period_lab) +
  scale_color_manual(values = team_colors) +
  labs(
    title = "Shot locations by period",
    subtitle = "Vancouver at Colorado, April 1, 2026",
    color = "Team"
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 18) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 22),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 14),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )









geom_hockey(league = "NHL") +
  geom_point(
    data = avs_vs_canucks,
    aes(x = arenaAdjustedXCord, y = arenaAdjustedYCord),
    color = "gray75",
    alpha = 0.45,
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = goal_df,
    aes(
      x = arenaAdjustedXCord,
      y = arenaAdjustedYCord,
      color = team_label
    ),
    size = 4.5
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ period_lab) +
  scale_color_manual(values = team_colors) +
  labs(
    title = "Goals highlighted over all shots",
    subtitle = "Vancouver at Colorado, April 1, 2026",
    color = "Team"
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 18) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 22),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 14),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )









avs_vs_canucks |>
  count(period_lab, team_label, event_label) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = period_lab, y = n, fill = event_label)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  facet_wrap(~ team_label) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Shot" = "#9ecae1", "Goal" = "#f28e2b")) +
  labs(
    title = "Shot and goal events by period",
    subtitle = "Vancouver at Colorado, April 1, 2026",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Events",
    fill = "Event type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 22),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 14),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 11),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )









van_heatmap <- shots_df |>
  filter(
    homeTeamCode == "COL",
    awayTeamCode == "VAN",
    game_id == 21188,
    period %in% c(1, 2, 3),
    event %in% c("SHOT", "GOAL"),
    teamCode == "VAN",
    !is.na(arenaAdjustedXCord),
    !is.na(arenaAdjustedYCord)
  )

geom_hockey(league = "NHL", display_range = "ozone") +
  stat_density_2d_filled(
    data = van_heatmap,
    aes(
      x = arenaAdjustedXCord,
      y = arenaAdjustedYCord,
      fill = after_stat(level)
    ),
    contour_var = "density",
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(25, 100), ylim = c(-42.5, 42.5)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(direction = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Vancouver offensive-zone shot density",
    subtitle = "Vancouver at Colorado, April 1, 2026",
    fill = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 18) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 22),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 14),
    legend.position = "right"
  )

title: NHL Shot Analysis
text: This project explores where NHL teams generate and convert shots using data from the 2025-26 regular season. I combine play by play event data with MoneyPucks shot-locaton coordinates. After building a Shiny app to interactivly filter games, periods and events, I focus on a case study of Vancouver at Colorado on April 1, 2026 to look at how shot location and volume change over three periods. Faceted shot maps, event counts, and an offensive zone density heatmap show that Vancouver increasingly attacked the goaltenders stick side, and scored most of their goals from this area, while Colorado’s shots remained more dispersed. These findings show how combining public NHL play by play data and coordinates can reveal patterns in how teams choose to shoot.

title: NHL Shot Analysis
text:
Data Description
In this project, I used two primary data sources covering the 2025-26 NHL season. The first is a play by play dataset obtained through the R package nhlscraper which contains event level information about every game, including shot attempts, goals, penalties, and game context. The second data source is from Moneypuck.com and includes shot-locations through x y rink coordinates, event type, team identifiers, and period information for every recorded shot of the same season.
From the play by play data, I focus on events where a shot was taken or a goal was scores, and use variables such ad gameId, isHome, period, shotType, strengthState, and rink coordinates (xCoord, yCoord). Other features are created such as attacking side, estimated angle to the net, and the distance to the net. From the Moneypuck data, I use the adjusted coordinates, event type, home/away team codes, and an indicator for if the event resulted in a goal.
Both data sources index games differently. Moneypuck uses a game_id starting at 1 for each season, and the play by play data uses a gameId starting at 2025000001. Mapping these together allows the Shiny app and visualizations to filter consistantly by game and combine angle information with precise shot coordinates.

title: NHL Shot Analysis
text:
Plots
To look at these patterns across all games in the 2025-26 NHL season, I build a Shiny app that links the two data sources and lets the user pick any home and away team, select a specific game between them, and filter by period and shot result (GOAL, SHOT, MISS). For the selected settings, the app updates three views: An intercative shot map with shooting angles, a shot-density heatmap, and a bar chart of shot events by period and team.









First we have a map of all shots on goal taken by each team for each period. This plot is actually not in my Shiny app, there is instead a more detailed plotly version of it with spokes showing the shot angle. I’m quite stumped on why it was struggling to move from there to here, however I believe it was because it is based on a different data set than the other ones. The plot you see here was instead taken from my presentation. It features geom_points() to show where shots were taken, each period, and is most effective when paired with the following plot (also from my presentation) to show which of those shots went in.


















Next, we have this bar plot to further communicate what happened during those periods, as counting dots can be rather challenging. This helps quantify those shots, and the ones that went in.









Finally, we have a heat map. This is using shots that didnt go in marked as 0, and goals marked as 1. you can see that during this game, the Canucks had most of their goals come from the goalies right side. The Avalanch goalie for the majority of this game was Mackenzie Blackwood, a goalie who wears his glove on his left hand. Targeting his stick side was clearly much more successful for the Canucks

title: NHL Shot Analysis
text:
Conclusion
Overall, combining play by play data with Poneypuck shot coordinates shows that Vancouvers offense in this particular game against Colorado relied heavily on generating shots from the goalies right side. Across the periods, the shot maps and bar chart show that vancouver increased both shot volume and finishing from this area as the game progressed, while colorado’s attempts remained more dispersed and less efficient. The offensive zone heatmap suggests this wasn’t a random pattern. The Canucks repeatedly targeted Blackwood’s stick side rather than spreading shots evenly. These results are limited by the focus on a single game, and not taking into account the goalie with stats like expected goals.
